title: Content to seem foolish
hookLine: if you want to improve, be willing to look foolish about outside things (Enchiridion 13)

lines: ZENO AND A POT OF SOUP.
cards: Athens. A merchant named Zeno, recently shipwrecked, has found a teacher: Crates the Cynic. One day, as Diogenes Laertius tells it, Crates hands him a pot of lentil soup to carry through the busy potters' quarter.
Zeno tries to hide the pot under his cloak, embarrassed. Crates cracks it with his staff, and soup runs down Zeno's legs. Zeno bolts.
Crates calls after him, roughly: why run away, little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you. Zeno would go on to found the Stoic school.

teach.b: Section thirteen of the handbook says: if you want to make progress, be content to be thought foolish and simple about outside things. Not foolish about everything.
About the outside things: the latest phone, the right restaurant, the gossip, who's up and who's down. Then the harder half.

teach.h: DON'T WISH TO SEEM TO KNOW.
teach.b: Don't wish to be thought to know anything, Epictetus says. And if people start to think you're somebody, be suspicious of yourself. That's a striking line from a well-known teacher.
It sounds like Socrates in Plato's Apology, who says he is wiser only in not thinking he knows what he doesn't.
The reason: it isn't easy, he says, to keep your purpose in line with nature and also keep up with all the outside things. Care for one, and you're bound to neglect the other.
Attention is limited. Spend it on looking clever and there's less left for being good. And it's training.
Looking foolish can feel like a small death: the red face, the wish to explain. That's exactly what Crates' soup pot was training.

Each time you survive it, you learn what Crates shouted: nothing terrible has happened. You asked the obvious question in the meeting, and the meeting went on. You wore last year's coat, and the sun came up.
You said I don't know, and someone finally explained it. People may think you're a little behind.
Let them think it. Your attention stays free for what's really yours.

how: Some Stoic practitioners deliberately accept looking uninformed or unfashionable about outside matters, as training in caring less about others' opinions.

o: the potter whose shop Zeno walked through
the founder of the Stoic school in Athens
the Cynic teacher who cracked Zeno's pot of soup

games.q: content to seem foolish — tap the pairs.
p: didn't think he knew what he didn't

s: Epictetus says be willing to look foolish about everything
about outside things; your purpose is where your attention goes.
the story of Zeno and the soup comes from Diogenes Laertius
his Lives of the Philosophers tells it in the life of Zeno.
section thirteen says if people think you're somebody, trust it
it says be suspicious of yourself.

games.q: you're Zeno. soup is running down your legs in the potters' quarter. what do you do?
games.why: Zeno ran. Crates called after him: nothing terrible has happened to you. the lesson stuck; Zeno founded the Stoic school.

practice: Picture one place where you usually perform knowing, a meeting, a class, a conversation you're supposed to follow, and see yourself asking the simple question, or saying, I don't actually know what that means.
Feel the flush of it rise and pass. Then hear Crates' line, gently this time: nothing terrible has happened.

wordCard.voice: Crates, the Cynic who cracked Zeno's soup pot to teach him this: let people think you simple about outside things, and keep your attention for what's yours. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: let them think it. A red face passes, and the meeting goes on. Day three hundred forty-five, done.

sources.work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers
